newsitem.title: CANADA: Historic Montreal statues on the auction block.
newsitem.headline: Historic Montreal statues on the auction block.

text.p: Defenders of Montreal's eroding architectural heritage have appealed to authorities to prevent the sale of four historic statues on the auction block.
Four 15-foot (4.5-metre) limestone statues created by New York City sculptor H. Augustus Lukeman 90 years ago are scheduled to be sold at auction on Tuesday.
The sculptures, four women representing Montreal's mercantile past -- industry, transportation, fishing and agriculture -- will be sold to repay an overdue storage bill.

The owner of the warehouse where the statues were stored seized them for non-payment of the bill. Members of Heritage Montreal, a private foundation working to protect the city's architectural heritage, are worried the statues will be sold to American or European buyers who have expressed interest in them.
"We don't want to see them end up in some guy's garden in Connecticut," said Nancy Dunton, executive director of the foundation.
With time running out, preservationists are appealing to the municipal and Quebec governments to intervene before the auction, as the cost of doing so would be much greater afterward.
City hall official Gilles Morelle said that Montreal had asked Quebec's Culture Minister Louise Beaudoin to designate the statues as part of the province's cultural heritage.
"That means the works could not be taken outside Quebec," Morelle said, but not prevent the auction.
The statues, inspired by the Ecole Francaise movement at the turn of the century, were part of the facade of a massive stone building that was the original headquarters of the Royal Bank of Canada.
They were removed in 1990 in preparation for the redevelopment of the building into a hotel, but the developer went bankrupt, abandoning the building and the statues.

Worried Montrealers say the statues' plight is symbolic of the disappearance of the 354-year-old city's architectural heritage. In recent decades, scores of historic buildings in "Old Montreal" have been demolished, burned down or abandoned as the city's financial sector moved westward toward its more modern downtown.
